final_answer:
In a free market, the interaction of supply and demand establishes the price of goods and services. When the quantity of a product that suppliers are willing to provide at a given price matches the quantity consumers want to purchase, the market reaches equilibrium. If demand exceeds supply, prices rise, encouraging producers to supply more and consumers to buy less. Conversely, if supply exceeds demand, prices fall, prompting producers to reduce output and consumers to buy more. This dynamic ensures resources are allocated based on willingness to pay and production costs.

When a government imposes a price ceiling—setting a maximum price below the equilibrium level—it disrupts this balance. Suppliers may reduce production because the price is too low to cover costs, while consumers, faced with lower prices, increase demand. This creates a shortage, as the quantity demanded exceeds the quantity supplied. Over time, this can lead to black markets, reduced product quality, or rationing, as the artificial constraint prevents the market from self-correcting. If the price ceiling is set above the equilibrium, however, it has no effect on the market.
